newsitem.title: UK: Six IRA men get 35 years for London blackout plot.
newsitem.headline: Six IRA men get 35 years for London blackout plot.

text.p: Six IRA activists were jailed for 35 years each on Wednesday for plotting to black out London on a scale unseen since World War Two.

The six, some of them said by the prosecution in a three-month trial to be senior commanders in the outlawed Irish Republican Army, were convicted of conspiracy to cause explosions likely to endanger life.

Prosecutors said the six planned to bomb electricity stations and paralyse power supplies to London and south-eastern England in 1996 to humiliate the British government because of its policy on Northern Ireland.
The defendants had denied the charges, claiming they were merely planning a hoax to force British authorities to shut down electricity supplies themselves, and cause chaos in the capital.

Gerard Hanratty, a self-confessed IRA activist, broke tradition to tell the court that the "brilliant" plan would have hurt (then Prime Minister) John Major and the British government and ridiculed tight security measures around the city of London financial district.
He said the IRA, which is fighting against British rule of Northern Ireland, had intended to bring more chaos to London than at any time since the Blitz during World War Two.

"The electrical impact would be total disruption in London. All the traffic lights would be out. It would result in chaos. All industries would be starved -- rail, tube and travel," Hanratty told the court.

The prosecution said six bombs were to be attached to transformers at each of the six electricity power stations ringing London in what the IRA had intended to be its biggest operation since the end of its 17-month ceasefire six months previously in February 1996.
"It was the most sophisticated plan they have ever launched," anti-terrorist police chief Commander John Grieve told the court.
The gang was arrested in London in July 1996 after a surveillance operation by police and secret service agents as the activists prepared for a practice run.

The arrests followed a huge IRA bomb in the northern city of Manchester the previous month in which more than 200 people were injured, and a February bomb attack in London's Docklands commercial district in February which killed two and shattered the IRA ceasefire.
During raids on IRA hideouts in the capital in which another suspected IRA activist was shot dead by police, officers recovered 37 timers and power units.
The five others convicted were Donald Gannon, 33, Patrick Martin, 34, Robert Morrow, 36, Francis Rafferty, 44 and John Crawley, 39. Two other men were found not guilty of the charges.
